headline: Sampling bias confounds machine learning prediction of antimicrobial resistance
label: Antimicrobial Resistance Prediction Benchmarking
summary: A published analysis of over 24,000 bacterial genomes shows phylogenetic and sampling-bias confounds in machine learning AMR prediction.
synthesis: The dominant thread is how bacterial population structure and sampling design shape what computational models can learn from genomes. The published analysis reports that phylogenetic sample structure and human-disease sampling bias confound machine learning prediction of antimicrobial resistance across more than 24,000 bacterial genomes. Two preprints extend the same population-genomic lens beyond benchmarking. One pools sequencing to profile millions of plasmid bases in E. coli, reporting sequence-encoded host interactions that govern plasmid propagation, and introduces the TRACE neural network. The other offers a reusable Wright-Fisher-based model with negative frequency-dependent selection on the accessory genome, explaining pneumococcal vaccine replacement and informing surveillance timing. What is new is treating sampling and selection as explicit determinants of model validity, rather than treating prediction accuracy as a property of the algorithm alone.
